indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2. 5.2.1: Know common diseases of humans, causes, symptoms, effects and prevention
indicator.objective: Identify causes and prevention of ringworm

misconceptions: Ringworm is caused by a real worm.
Ringworm is caused by a curse or witchcraft.
You can only get ringworm if you are visibly dirty.
Sharing a towel or comb is safe because it is just for grooming.
Ringworm will go away on its own without any treatment.

questions.explanation: Ringworm is caused by a fungus (germ), not a real worm.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think ringworm is caused by a real worm.

questions.stem: What does ringworm look like on the skin?
hints: It is shaped like a ring.
questions.explanation: Ringworm appears as a red, circular, itchy patch on the skin.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think it looks like a worm.

options: Keep your skin clean and dry
questions.explanation: Keeping your skin clean and dry helps prevent ringworm.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not link hygiene to ringworm prevention.

questions.stem: Which of these can cause ringworm to spread?
options: Sharing a towel with an infected person
questions.explanation: Sharing a towel or comb with an infected person can spread the ringworm fungus.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize skin diseases spread through shared items.

questions.stem: What should you do if you think you have ringworm?
options: Tell a parent and go to a clinic
hints: A health worker can give medicine.
questions.explanation: You should tell a parent and go to a clinic for treatment.

questions.stem: Ama says 'Ringworm is caused by a real worm.' Is she right?
options: No, it is caused by a germ (fungus)
Yes, it is a small insect
No, it is caused by a curse
hints: Do you see a worm in the patch?
questions.explanation: Ama is not right. Ringworm is caused by a fungus, not a real worm.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think ringworm is a literal worm.

questions.stem: Kwame has a round, red, itchy patch on his arm. What might it be?
questions.explanation: A round, red, itchy patch on the skin is a common sign of ringworm.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse ringworm with other diseases.

questions.stem: Why should you not share your towel with a friend who has ringworm?
options: The towel might be too small
The germs can transfer from their skin to the towel and then to you
questions.explanation: Sharing a towel with an infected person can spread the ringworm fungus to you.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think sharing is always safe.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a cause of ringworm?
hints: Which one does not affect the skin?
Sugar is food, not a skin germ.
questions.explanation: Eating too much sugar does not cause ringworm. Ringworm is caused by a fungus and spreads through poor hygiene and shared items.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think food causes skin diseases.

questions.stem: Ama has ringworm. What should she do with her towel and clothes?
options: Wash them separately with hot water and soap
questions.explanation: Ama should wash her towel and clothes separately with hot water and soap to kill the fungus and prevent spreading.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know how to prevent spreading.

questions.stem: What type of germ causes ringworm?
hints: It grows in warm, moist places.
questions.explanation: Ringworm is caused by a fungus.

questions.stem: Describe what ringworm looks like on the skin.
questions.explanation: Ringworm appears as a round, red, itchy patch on the skin.
questions.misconception: Pupils may describe it as a worm.

questions.stem: Why is it important to dry your body properly after bathing to prevent ringworm?
options: Because the fungus grows well in warm, wet places
hints: Dry skin is less welcoming to fungus.
questions.explanation: Ringworm fungus thrives in warm, moist areas. Drying your body properly removes moisture and helps prevent infection.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize moisture encourages fungal growth.

questions.stem: A student says 'Only poor people get ringworm.' Why is this statement wrong?
options: Ringworm is caused by a fungus, not by poverty; anyone can get it if they come into contact with the germ
Ringworm is not a real disease
questions.explanation: Ringworm is caused by a fungus, and anyone can get it regardless of wealth if they come into contact with the germ.
questions.misconception: Pupils may associate diseases with poverty.

questions.stem: Write down two ways to prevent ringworm.

criteria.description: States keeping the skin clean and dry
States not sharing personal items like towels or combs

hints: What should your skin be like?
questions.explanation: Prevention includes keeping skin clean and dry, and not sharing personal items.

questions.stem: Explain how ringworm spreads from one person to another.

criteria.description: States that the fungus can be on shared items like towels, combs, or clothes
States that touching these items or the infected person's skin can pass the germ on

questions.explanation: Ringworm spreads when a person touches the infected skin or shares items like towels, combs, or clothes that have the fungus on them.

questions.stem: A family shares one towel in the bathroom. One child gets ringworm. What is the BEST action to stop it from spreading?
options: Give each person their own towel and wash them separately
Use the same towel but wash it once a month
Ignore it because it will go away
questions.explanation: Giving each person their own towel and washing them separately prevents the fungus from spreading to others.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize shared items spread disease.

questions.stem: Explain why ringworm is NOT caused by a worm, even though it is called 'ringworm'.

criteria.description: States that it is caused by a fungus (germ)
States that the name comes from the ring-shaped rash, not a worm

hints: Look at the shape of the rash.
It is a germ, not an animal.
questions.explanation: Ringworm is caused by a fungus, not a worm. It is called ringworm because the rash forms a ring shape on the skin.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher what you would do if you saw a round, itchy patch on your skin.

criteria.description: States they would tell a parent or teacher
States they would go to a clinic for treatment

questions.explanation: You should tell an adult and seek medical treatment for the rash.
